claim: Cole et al.'s 2026 Science paper on Galápagos corals finds that eastern Pacific ENSO variability since 1984 is 36.5% above 1000 to 1850 CE, outside the range of 12 climate models' natural variability, and that the growth comes from stronger El Niños.
source_title: Recent strengthening of eastern Pacific ENSO in the last millennium paleorecord (Science, 2026)
passage: The geochemistry of Galápagos coral skeletons across the past millennium reveals a large recent increase in interannual variability of sea surface temperature in the eastern equatorial Pacific compared with that in existing paleorecords that exceeds simulated natural variability. This increase parallels rising global temperature and results from stronger El Niño events. Central Pacific coral data also show increased variability, although less distinctly than in the Galápagos.
notes: Only the abstract is readable; the 36.5% figure and the 12-model comparison are in the paywalled full text (the card took the number from the AAAS release and Ars).

claim: Wright, Bosma and Lopez-Cantu (GRL 2019) found that from 1950 to 2017 in the eastern U.S. 2-year storm exceedances rose 51% but 500-year exceedances rose 301%, and that by 2017 the Atlas 14 '100-year' storm recurred more often than every 100 years in every region but the Southwest.

passage: We computed 2017 observed ARIs for eight NOAA climate regions using the mean of Atlas 14, as well as TP40 for 100-year, 24-hr rainfall exceedances (Figures 4b and 4c). In 2017, in all regions except West (Southwest), observed ARIs are below 100 years relative to the Atlas 14 mean (TP40) IDF estimates
notes: The 51%/301% figures are correct (section 3.1), but against the Atlas 14 mean the exception is the West, not the Southwest (Southwest is the TP40 exception; the paper gives the Southwest a 2017 observed ARI of 76 years). Fetched via Exa; wiley blocks curl.

claim: NOAA's Climate Prediction Center replaced the 30-year-baseline Oceanic Niño Index as its official ENSO index because the ONI 'struggles to keep pace' with changes in tropical sea surface temperature.
source_title: CPC adopts Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) for reliable, responsive monitoring and tracking of ENSO (NOAA CPC)
passage: The Climate Prediction Center is making the shift to use the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) to better designate past events and predict future ENSO. The traditional Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) relies on a departure from 30-year average that struggles to keep pace with anomalous changes in tropical sea surface temperature (SST), which is particularly problematic in real-time when using a time lagged climatology. RONI solves this problem by comparing the ENSO region to the global tropics, thereby reducing the dependency on the climate base period.
notes: Card also gives the date (February 2026) and the reclassification of past events, which come from the linked circular rather than this paragraph.

claim: NOAA is replacing Atlas 14's stationary precipitation-frequency estimates with a nonstationary Atlas 15 that adds future adjustment factors from climate models.
source_title: NOAA Atlas 15 (NOAA NWS Office of Water Prediction)
passage: NOAA Atlas 15 can help communities nationwide become more resilient when planning and designing new infrastructure. This objective will be supported by (1) the delivery of spatially continuous precipitation frequency estimates that cover the entire United States and (2) the incorporation of nonstationary statistical methods and information from climate models to account for future trends. Although precipitation frequency estimates have existed for many decades (since the late 1930s) and have incrementally improved with advancements in data, science and technology, NOAA Atlas 15 represents a shift from a stationary assumption (i.e., extreme precipitation events do not change significantly over time) to a nonstationary assumption (i.e., extreme precipitation events change over time), a key modification that may impact the manner in which precipitation frequency information is applied.

claim: Wilks (Journal of Applied Meteorology and Climatology, 2013) found in hindcasts that plain 15- and 30-year averages beat shorter windows and that trend (hinge) fits were 'not yet justified'.
source_title: Projecting "Normals" in a Nonstationary Climate (Wilks, JAMC 2013)
passage: Climate “normals” are statistical estimates of present and/or near-future climate means for such quantities as seasonal temperature or precipitation. In a changing climate, simply averaging a large number of previous years of data may not be the best method for estimating normals. Here eight formulations for climate normals, including the recently proposed “hinge” function, are compared in artificial- and real-data settings. Although the hinge function is attractive conceptually for representing accelerating climate changes simply, its use is in general not yet justified for divisional U.S. seasonal temperature or precipitation. Averages of the most recent 15 and 30 yr have performed better during the recent past for U.S. divisional seasonal temperature and precipitation, respectively; these averaging windows are longer than those currently employed for this purpose at the U.S. Climate Prediction Center.
notes: Card also says tuned windows did worse; that is in the paper's conclusions ('yielded inferior results'), not the abstract.

claim: The Census Bureau's August 2026 brief 'Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election, A Beginning Analysis' validates the DataClear voter file with a comparison it calls 'one of magnitude, not of individuals.'
source_title: Noncitizen Voting in the 2020 Election, A Beginning Analysis (U.S. Census Bureau)
passage: External validation of the voter file. Because this beginning brief rests on the DataClear file, the file is checked against an independent official benchmark: the U.S. Election Assistance Commission’s Election Administration and Voting Survey (EAVS) for 2020, the federal government’s compilation of turnout counts certified by state election offices (U.S. Election Assistance Commission 2023). The comparison is one of magnitude, not of individuals. DataClear’s count of people flagged as having voted in 2020 is a count of ballots cast, which is what the EAVS item F1a measures, and the brief compares the two directly. Nationally, DataClear captures 146,700,000 of the 159,934,200 ballots the states reported to the EAVS across the fifty states and the District of Columbia, or 91.7 percent.
notes: Passage from the brief's PDF linked on the page. Card also lists absences (no false match rate, no confidence intervals, no authors), which can only be checked against the whole brief.

claim: Charles Stewart's newsletter post on the Census noncitizen voting brief notes that in earlier research an estimate of about 33,000 double voters could be explained by a 1.3% clerical error rate.

passage: Their initial model estimated approximately 33,000 double voters. But Goel et al. didn’t stop there. They investigated whether the commercial vote histories were accurate. By comparing electronic records with Philadelphia poll books, they found that clerical errors could produce the appearance of double voting. An error rate of only 1.3% would have been sufficient to explain nearly all of their estimated double votes.
notes: Card sentence also gives ADGN's 2.2% false positive rate, which is in an earlier paragraph of the same post.

claim: My Community Data reported in March 2026 that of roughly 365 HIFLD Open services, about 52 still respond, and that the survivors are hosted by the agencies that produce them.

The surviving services are overwhelmingly hosted on agency-owned servers (USGS, FEMA, NOAA, EPA, USACE, Census) rather than the centralized HIFLD ArcGIS organization. notes: This card has no Evidence sections; claims taken from its 'Why now' bullets (each names one source) and then 'Their words'. Page is JS-rendered; text fetched via Exa.

claim: The Data Rescue Project announced on 2025-12-15 that 415 HIFLD Open layers were archived in DataLumos, useful for 'the next couple of years' before becoming a historic archive.

It will be useful for data users and mappers who need easily accessible and relatively current data for the next couple of years; after that, it will serve primarily as a historic archive.

claim: Business News Today reported on 2026-08-13 that UK Power Networks directly monitors about 14% of its 120,000+ secondary transformers and that its 96.7% figure measures network-visibility forecast accuracy, not failure prediction.

claim: Hugging Face's write-up of the July 2026 agent intrusion says the agent picked Hugging Face as a target because it 'inferred that Hugging Face may host that benchmark's models, datasets, and reference solutions.'

passage: The operator selected targets in several ways. passage: The Community Layer can be used to tie Community ID numbers (CID) to jurisdiction, tribal, and special land use area boundaries. However, as jurisdictions may change over time, this dataset should not be considered authoritative. Data as of December 2024. No updates are planned at this time.
